drills.title: A shopping cart that grows
drills.prompt: Arrange the lines into a program that builds a cart, replaces the bread and prints the cart. The two imports can go in either order. Two lines do not belong.
drills.explain: Write the variable's type as the interface List<String> and create the real list with new ArrayList<>(). List alone is only a description and cannot be created with new. Lists have no square-bracket access: you read with get(i) and replace with set(i, value). The imports come first, before the class.

drills.title: Collections helpers and sets
drills.prompt: Fill the blanks so the program prints the goal output.
drills.explain: Collections is the helper class for lists: max gives the biggest value and frequency counts how often a value appears (95 twice). A set keeps every value only once, so copying the list into a HashSet and asking for size() counts the different marks (3). contains answers true or false, while indexOf would print a position.

drills.title: Position or value?
drills.prompt: Read the code and type exactly what it prints, one line per line of output.
drills.explain: remove(1) has an int inside, so it removes the item at position 1 (the 95). remove(Integer.valueOf(60)) has an Integer, so it removes the value 60. add on a set says true only the first time. Integer objects above 127 are separate objects, so == is false while equals is true: always compare wrapper types with equals.

drills.title: A menu that refuses new items
drills.prompt: The shop wants to add jalebi to its menu list, but the program crashes while it runs. Click the line that has to change (not the line that crashes) and choose the fix.
drills.explain: List.of makes a list that can never change: add, remove and set all throw UnsupportedOperationException. The crash shows at line 6, but the cause is how the list was made. Copy it into an ArrayList when you need changes. List.copyOf is read-only too.

drills.title: Review the AI's mutual friends
drills.prompt: An AI assistant wrote this friends program. It compiles and runs, but tick the real problems (there are three).

issues.text: retainAll changes mine itself, so the later union is wrong and aarav is missing from Everyone
issues.why: retainAll, addAll and removeAll change the set they are called on. Work on a copy: Set<String> both = new HashSet<>(mine); both.retainAll(hers);

issues.text: The line says A-Z but a HashSet makes no promise about order
issues.why: Never rely on HashSet order. Copy into a TreeSet (new TreeSet<>(all)) when the report must be sorted.

issues.text: unique.contains(v) walks the whole list on every round, which gets slow for millions of visits
issues.why: contains on a list looks at items one by one. A HashSet seen finds an item almost instantly: if (seen.add(v)) { unique.add(v); } keeps the order and stays fast.

non_issues.text: new HashSet<>(List.of(...)) is pointless: use Set.of(...) directly
non_issues.why: Set.of is read-only, so retainAll and addAll would throw UnsupportedOperationException. Copying into a HashSet gives a changeable set.

non_issues.text: mine should be declared as HashSet<String>, not Set<String>
non_issues.why: Declaring the variable with the interface and creating the class on the right is the recommended Java habit.

non_issues.text: unique.add(v) changes a list while the loop is running
non_issues.why: The loop walks over visits and the code adds to unique, which is a different list. Only changing the looped list would be a problem.

drills.explain: Set operations that change the set in place, unordered HashSets and list.contains in a loop are the typical collection slips of generated code. All of them compile and produce believable output on three items.
